references.text: Describes the actual sale of Joseph to the Ishmaelites/Midianites, as a direct follow-up to Judah's proposal.
Joseph's brothers reflect with remorse on their guilt in what they did to Joseph, including that they sold him.
The expression 'flesh and blood' is used regarding kinship, parallel to Judah's argument: 'he is after all our brother, our own flesh and blood'.
The psalmist refers to Joseph being sold as a slave, a poetic summary of the brothers' actions.
Judas Iscariot sells Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, a parallel to Joseph's brothers who sold him for silver.
In his speech, Stephen refers to how the patriarchs sold Joseph into Egypt out of jealousy, a direct reference to this event.
Nehemiah uses the story of Joseph as a moral mirror to condemn the exploitation of one's own brothers.
A direct continuation of the same sequence of events where the brothers must meet the demand to bring the youngest brother.
Jeremiah's lament that fathers did not heed God's command to free their brothers highlights the ethical breach in the story of Joseph.
The same narrative thread; the demand to bring Benjamin is the direct consequence of the brothers' earlier actions.
A direct part of the same story; the brothers' response to Joseph's question about the 'lost' brother.
The conclusion of the story of Joseph where the brothers admit their guilt after having sold him.
